sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.content: This report presents an in-depth analysis of 10 customer cases extracted from the CRM system (unformatted text exports) covering the period from May through December 2025, systematically cross-referenced against the Services Guide and FAQ as the operational benchmark for evaluation. The report's purpose is not to present numbers but to transform raw data into actionable decisions that address root causes rather than surface symptoms. Core Discovery: Manual reclassification revealed that the CRM had labelled 100% of the ten cases as 'inquiries', while rigorous review confirmed that 60% were in fact disguised complaints and requests — meaning the system was being managed on the basis of a wholly distorted picture of the nature of customer interactions.

subsections.title: Key Findings
subsections.content: Core Message: The systemic failure the data exposes is not in the volume of cases but in the information architecture — a system that misclassifies 60% of its interactions, operates with a guidebook that covers on average only 32% of actual customer needs, and maintains a digital channel rate of zero, is a system managing reactively rather than proactively. Correcting the classification alone enables the activation of 6 proactive notification scenarios (60% of total cases) that would sever the cycle of repeat contact before it occurs. What this reclassification exercise unlocks is not merely a periodic report — but a trustworthy data platform on which a prevention-led, digitally-enabled service strategy can be built.

rows.Discovery: 60% Misclassification Rate Corrupts the Entire Operational Database
rows.Description: The audit revealed that 6 out of 10 cases were incorrectly classified under the 'inquiry' label which had been assigned to the entire sample, while the corrected classification showed the actual distribution as: inquiries (4), complaints (4), and requests (2). No comparative data from prior periods is available to measure the trend over time; however, the 60% rate represents a critical data quality gap that renders any decision built on current system outputs fundamentally unsound.

rows.Discovery: Inquiries and Complaints Each at 40% — With Complete Absence of Complaint Subcategory Data
rows.Description: Inquiries are the dominant category at 4 cases (40%), yet they share an equal footing with complaints which also reached 4 cases (40%) — a finding that directly contradicts the original CRM classification suggesting 100% were inquiries. More critically, complaint subcategory data is entirely absent, meaning the system holds zero granular visibility into the subject matter of complaints — the operationally highest-priority category.

rows.Discovery: 2 Cases with No Digital Path: Absence of Proactive Notifications on Weapon Licence Applications Generates Repeat Contact
rows.Description: The absence of automated status updates on weapon licence applications has led customers to make repeated contact to inquire about the progress of their applications — a consistent pattern representing 2 cases, the highest single-friction-point volume in the entire sample. Analysis reveals that the services guide is completely devoid of any content relating to weapon licensing or application tracking mechanisms (match confidence: 0.05); with no digital self-service inquiry channel available, customers are compelled to contact the centre directly at every stage of application processing.

rows.Discovery: 5 Cases Stemming from Information Entirely Absent from the Services Guide — All Preventable
rows.Description: Five friction points share the same root cause — missing information (missing_info) — spanning: customers' unawareness of Fujairah licence validity across the UAE (1 case), unclear traffic fine discount mechanisms (1 case), ignorance of inter-emirate speed tolerance differences (1 case), repeated appeals filed without prior knowledge of discount procedures (1 case), and ambiguity over the correct channel for vehicle destruction certificates (1 case). Data confirms that the current guidebook's average coverage for this cluster does not exceed 32%, and that adding structured, well-categorised content on these topics alone is sufficient to prevent recurring friction cases without any technical fix.

rows.Discovery: 100% On-Time Closure Rate — High Execution Capacity Against a Structural Gap
rows.Description: All ten cases were closed within the stipulated service level, representing a 100% on-time closure rate with no exceptions. However, this operational performance, commendable as it is, addresses cases after they have arisen rather than treating the structural causes that generated them in the first place — particularly in the context of a 0% digital channel rate; this reflects superior execution capacity that should not be consumed in handling cases that could have been prevented.

rows.Nature: CRM data with unstructured text fields (case details, resolutions, service names, case descriptions)
Official reference covering traffic, licensing, and security services, plus FAQ validation and gap analysis

subsections.title: 2.2 Classification Methodology
subsections.content: The classification methodology employed a two-stage pipeline applied to all ten cases. In Stage 1, the rule-based engine (stage2_rules.py) applied a prioritised decision tree in the following order: (1) Objection to a traffic violation, (2) Submission of a security or traffic report, (3) Request for a weapons permit or licence, (4) Complaint regarding non-receipt of service, (5) Complaint regarding a technical or system error, (6) Complaint regarding processing delay, (7) Inquiry about licences and vehicles, (8) Commendation and praise, with a fallback to the CRM's نوع_المكالمة label when none of the above priorities applied. The confidence threshold was set at 0.75; cases meeting or exceeding this threshold were classified directly, while cases falling below it were queued for Stage 2. In Stage 2, the large language model engine (stage3_llm.py), using the model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 via tool-use, was applied to cases rejected by the rule engine — zero cases in this batch. Cases for which the LLM confidence fell below 0.65 were routed to a human review queue and excluded from report counts, amounting to zero cases as well. All classification across both stages was governed by a two-level taxonomy comprising four top-level types (Complaint, Request, Inquiry, Commendation and Praise), each decomposed into domain-specific sub-classifications totalling 25 sub-types. The foundational definitional principle governing this methodology is that the nature of what is sought — not the phrasing — is the decisive criterion: a case expressing dissatisfaction is classified as a complaint even if it contains a request for action.

subsections.title: 2.3 Analyzed Fields
subsections.content: The fields processed in this analysis are divided into two principal groups. The first group comprises the structured fields, which are handled independently by the dashboard and visual analytics tools (PowerBI) and are not subject to the text-classification pipeline; these fields are: Request Number (رقم_الطلب), Creation Date (تاريخ_الإنشاء), Service Submission Channel (قناة_تقديم_الخدمة), Main Service (الخدمة_الرئيسية), Call Type (نوع_المكالمة), Nationality (الجنسية), and Responsible Department (الإدارة_المختصة). The second group, which constitutes the focus of this analysis, comprises the unstructured free-text fields: the Case Details field (تفاصيل_الطلب), with an average length of 434 characters and a language distribution of 72% Arabic and 28% English; and the Resolution field (الحل), with an average length of 102 characters and the same language distribution. Together, these two fields reveal the true nature of each case beyond the original label recorded in the CRM's Call Type field (نوع_المكالمة).
